soil-chem-058.title: Humic substances, the dark core of soil organic matter
soil-chem-058.text: Most soil organic matter is not fresh leaves or roots but something darker and older. Humic substances are dark, relatively decay-resistant organic compounds that form as biomass residues break down and change over long periods. They make up most of the organic material in soil, {{ref:soil-class-070}}, coal and sediments, and much of the organic material dissolved in lakes, rivers and sea water. Their color runs from bright yellow through brown to black, and the name comes from the Latin word for 'soil, earth'. Microbes make them from dead material such as {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, cellulose and charred wood. Yet how they form is among the least understood parts of the chemistry of soil organic matter. Maillard proposed a sugar-amine condensation theory in 1911, and Waksman, in 1932, a theory built on that woody compound. Those formed in soil over hundreds to thousands of years carry more oxygen and nitrogen than those from coal, formed over millions. Chemists split them by solubility into three fractions. They also supply 50 to 90% of a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-069.title: Chelation: how molecules grip metals like a claw
soil-chem-069.text: A crab holds its prey with two pincers, and some molecules hold metal atoms the same way. Chelation is the bonding of a metal atom by a molecule that grips it at two or more points, closing a ring. The name comes from the Greek chēlē, 'claw', and Morgan and Drew first used the word 'chelate' in 1920. The gripping molecule, or ligand, is called a chelant, chelator, chelating agent or sequestering agent. It is usually organic, though it need not be. Most metal complexes in nature sit in some kind of chelate ring, held by a humic substance or a protein. In soil, these chelates govern how metals move. They also control how plants and microorganisms take up and store metals. As a negatively charged colloid, {{ref:soil-bio-089}} raises a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and so its ability to store nutrients by chelation. People use the same grip in nutritional supplements, chelation therapy for toxic metals, MRI contrast agents, catalysts, water treatment and fertilizers. The process can also run backward. In dechelation, acidifying the solution with a mineral acid forms a precipitate and recovers the chelating agent.

soil-chem-068.title: Sorption: the many ways one substance sticks to another
soil-chem-068.text: Some soil organic matter is more than a century old, and part of the reason is that it is stuck. Sorption is any physical and chemical process by which one substance becomes attached to another. It covers absorption into a substance of a different state, adsorption of ions and molecules onto the surface of another phase, and the swapping of ions. For a dilute solute, the rates of adsorption and absorption can be calculated with Fick's laws of diffusion. Much soil {{ref:soil-bio-089}} persists for over 100 years partly because it is tightly sorbed or bound to clays, out of reach of microbes and their enzymes. Sorption also steers nutrients. Molybdenum is sorbed most strongly in acid soils, so adding lime often relieves a shortage of molybdenum by loosening that hold. Aluminum sorbed onto exposed hydroxyl groups gives the edges of clay plates a slight positive charge. Those edges stick to the negative faces of other particles, and the clay flocculates. In {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, ammonium from {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, a strongly sorbing cation, trades places with weakly sorbing sodium and releases it into the water.

soil-chem-049.title: Variable charge: soil surfaces that shift with pH
soil-chem-049.text: Part of a soil's grip on nutrients turns up and down with acidity. Variable charge is surface charge on clay edges and soil organic matter that changes with the pH of the soil water. It comes from hydroxyl groups, pairs of oxygen and hydrogen atoms, that give up their hydrogen ions. The broken edges of clay sheets expose many acidic hydroxyl groups. At the pH of many soils these lose their hydrogen and leave negative charges behind. Soil organic matter does the same: hydrogens on its hydroxyl groups ionize into solution, leaving an oxygen with a negative charge. Its many charged groups give it a large share of a soil's power to hold cations, positively charged ions, and that share depends heavily on pH. Raising the pH means fewer hydrogen ions in solution. More groups then lose their hydrogen, the variable charge grows, and so does the {{ref:soil-chem-046}}.

soil-chem-073.title: Leonardite, the oxidized coal rich in humic acid
soil-chem-073.text: Lignite left near the surface slowly oxidizes into something else. Leonardite is a soft, waxy, black or brown mineraloid formed by the oxidation of lignite, and it dissolves easily in alkaline solutions. First described from North Dakota, it is named after A. G. Leonard, first director of the North Dakota Geological Survey. Up to 90% of it can be {{ref:soil-chem-059}}. It conditions soil when applied directly, or as a source of that acid or of {{ref:soil-chem-074}}. It also serves in water treatment, as a drilling additive and in the cleanup of polluted ground. Added to contaminated soil, especially with {{ref:soil-fert-028}}, it reduces the metals plants take up.

soil-chem-065.title: Making humic substances in hours instead of years
soil-chem-065.text: Nature needs years to make humic substances, and chemists can do it in hours. Artificial humic substances are humic-like materials made by people: by composting {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, adding {{ref:soil-fert-050}} or synthesizing them from organic feedstocks. Hydrothermal processing turns biomass in an alkaline solution at 180 °C–250 °C into all three humic fractions within minutes to hours. Oxidizing lignite does it too, reversing coal formation; China widely uses this 'mineral-derived' {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Such products have eased drought's effects on soil microbes and helped save a 160-year-old beech tree in Park Sanssouci, Potsdam.

soil-chem-062.title: Inside humic substances: thousands of molecules, no settled shape
soil-chem-062.text: Mass spectroscopy finds thousands of distinct components in humic material. Humic substances mix many molecules built from aromatic, aliphatic and carbohydrate units, carrying mainly carboxylic and phenolic groups. These groups supply most of the charge and reactivity, giving up hydrogen around pK 4 and pK 8, as in {{ref:soil-chem-049}}. They also bind Mg2+, Ca2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+, often as chelates, regulating how available those metals are. Molecular weights are lower than once thought. Researchers still disagree whether the molecules are large poly-condensates tied to clay or loose supramolecular associations of small ones.

soil-chem-064.title: Does organic matter feed plants? A dispute since the 18th century
soil-chem-064.text: People once believed plants fed directly on {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Then Liebig showed that plants grow on inorganic compounds, and soil organic matter came to be valued only for the nutrients it released as it broke down. Soil scientists now at least agree that it affects fertility by helping soil hold water. Its other effects on plants have been disputed since the 18th century. Plants may absorb soluble humic material, perhaps to take up iron, but this is not settled. Studies found humic products boosted growth even at low rates.

soil-chem-070.title: Why two grips beat one: the chelate effect
soil-chem-070.text: A molecule that holds a metal at two points beats two molecules holding it at one point each. That is the chelate effect: a chelating ligand's greater affinity for a metal ion than similar ligands that bind it only once. Bidentate, or two-pronged, ligands close a chelate ring around the metal, and as in organic chemistry, 5- and 6-membered rings predominate. Cadmium holds ethylenediamine, which forms a five-membered ring, far more strongly than two methylamine ligands of about the same donor power. The enthalpy changes, the heat given off, of the two reactions are about equal. So the advantage comes mainly from entropy, the measure of disorder.

soil-chem-072.title: Chelated fertilizers keep micronutrient metals in solution
soil-chem-072.text: The phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn trace metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants. Chelated micronutrient fertilizers avoid that trap by supplying manganese, iron, zinc and copper as metal chelates. EDTA is the typical chelating agent, and iron is often given as EDTA or EDDHA chelates. Sprayed on leaves, a chelated nutrient is absorbed and moved better, and less is lost to soil and groundwater. Use of EDTA and NTA is falling 6% a year over toxicity concerns, as greener EDDS and citrate gain ground.

soil-chem-071.title: Living chelators: how microbes and roots fetch metals
soil-chem-071.text: Living things make their own claws for metal. Natural chelating agents are molecules made by organisms that bind metal ions as chelates: proteins, polysaccharides, organic acids and microbial pigments. Malate, glutamic acid, histidine and the peptide phytochelatin are typical. Pseudomonas bacteria secrete the water-soluble pigments pyochelin and pyoverdine, which bind iron, and some root-dwelling bacteria use such pigments to hand iron to plants. Organic chelators such as peptides and sugars are even credited with chemical weathering, pulling metal ions out of rocks.

soil-chem-075.title: Point of zero charge, where a surface's sign flips
soil-chem-075.text: At one pH, a charged soil surface carries no net charge at all. That pH is its point of zero charge. Below it the surface turns positive and adsorbs anions, negatively charged ions; above it, the surface turns negative and adsorbs cations. The idea came from studies of colloid flocculation, since particles at this point flocculate fastest. Chemists find it by titrating a colloid suspension with acid and base. It governs how readily a surface adsorbs harmful ions, and even shifts soil emissions of nitrous acid.

soil-chem-060.title: Fulvic acid, the humic fraction that always dissolves
soil-chem-060.text: One fraction of humic substances dissolves in water at any pH, acid or alkaline. That fraction is fulvic acid. Compared with {{ref:soil-chem-059}}, it has more carboxylic groups, a lower average molecular weight and stronger acidity. Measured number-average molecular weights of fulvic acid from water are below 900. Fulvic acids hold more exchangeable cations, interact more strongly with fertilizers and form soluble chelates of trace metals. Those metal chelates are strongly leached and redeposited, an important part of cheluviation.

soil-chem-059.title: Humic acid, the fraction that strong acid leaves behind
soil-chem-059.text: Humic acid stays dissolved in neutral or alkaline water but not in strong acid. It is the fraction of humic substances that dissolves at neutral and alkaline pH but not below pH 2. It is a complex mixture of acids with carboxyl and phenolate groups that behaves as a dibasic acid, giving up two hydrogen ions, or occasionally three. Its number-average molecular weight is below 6000. {{ref:soil-fert-026}} lowers the pH of {{ref:soil-chem-019}} by generating humic acid. Its potassium salt, {{ref:soil-chem-074}}, comes from leonardite.

soil-chem-066.title: Humate, the humic rock that is mined
soil-chem-066.text: In New Mexico, soil amendment has been dug from the ground since the 1970s. The material is humate, which in economic geology means rock rich in humic acids. Weathered coal beds such as leonardite count, as do mudrock and the material filling pores in sandstone. The Fruitland Formation had produced nearly 60,000 metric tons of humate by 2016. Humate deposits may also play an important part in forming uranium ore bodies.

soil-chem-067.title: When humic acid meets chlorine in drinking water
soil-chem-067.text: Water from peaty uplands brings a chemistry problem to the treatment plant. Humic and fulvic acids react with chlorination chemicals to form disinfection byproducts such as dihaloacetonitriles, which are toxic to humans. So humic acid in water meant for drinking or industry affects how well that water can be treated and disinfected. Measuring it matters most for supplies drawn from upland peaty catchments in temperate climates. Exact measurement is cumbersome, so its concentration is usually estimated from total or dissolved organic carbon.

soil-chem-061.title: Splitting organic matter three ways with alkali and acid
soil-chem-061.text: In 1786 Franz Karl Achard treated {{ref:soil-class-070}} with potassium hydroxide, a strong alkali. Chemists still split natural organic material much the same way. Soil is extracted with 0.1 M NaOH under nitrogen to prevent oxidation, and the fraction left behind is {{ref:soil-bio-105}}. From natural waters, the acids are caught on a resin column at pH 2, and humic acid is then precipitated at pH 1. Commercial humic acid is made by these procedures. So humic substances are largely defined by the method used to extract them.

soil-chem-063.title: Do humic substances exist, or does the lab make them?
soil-chem-063.text: Since the 18th century, soil chemists have pulled organic material out of soil with alkali. That alkaline extraction led to a theory: a process called {{ref:soil-bio-090}} creates distinct humic acid, fulvic acid and {{ref:soil-bio-105}}. Critics now ask whether these substances exist in soil at all, or are made by the extraction itself. Modern analysis of unprocessed mineral soil has not directly observed large humic molecules. That suggests extraction alters the material it is meant to reveal. Because humic and fulvic acids are defined by the separation, it is unclear whether the categories reflect the natural state of soil organic matter. Some researchers argue that the method misrepresents humic substances because it uses highly alkaline extracts rather than water. Yet that theory persists, even in textbooks. Attempts to redefine humic substances have produced conflicting definitions, which hamper communication across the field. The question stays open: the old fractions may describe real soil, or they may be products of the flask.

soil-chem-074.title: Potassium humate, humic acid in granules
soil-chem-074.text: The best potassium humate starts as well-oxidized lignite. Potassium humate is the potassium salt of humic acid, made by alkaline extraction of leonardite and used mainly to condition soil. Makers extract it in hot water with potassium hydroxide and other agents, then dry it into granules that can be mixed into fertilizer. There it makes nitrogen and phosphorus inputs more efficient. Less oxidized coal yields less potassium humate, and low-ash sources give the best quality.

soil-chem-048.title: Permanent charge, locked into the clay crystal
soil-chem-048.text: Some of a clay's charge is fixed the moment the clay forms. Permanent charge is negative charge built into a clay's crystal where atoms of lower charge replace atoms of higher charge. In layered clays of aluminum and silicon oxides, Mg2+ taking the place of Al3+ leaves a net negative charge. This isomorphous substitution never changes with time, and it releases no hydrogen ions, so the charge ignores pH. Kaolinite has almost no substitution and a low cation-holding power, while montmorillonite owes its power to magnesium replacing aluminum.

soil-chem-047.title: Cation exchange: how soil trades nutrients with its water
soil-chem-047.text: Calcium, potassium and ammonium do not simply wash through a good soil. They cling to it, loosely, and trade places with other ions in the soil water. That trading is cation exchange: negatively charged sites on soil colloids attract positively charged ions and swap them with ions in solution. It is one case of ion exchange, a reversible swap of like-charged ions between an insoluble solid and the surrounding solution. Natural exchangers include zeolites, montmorillonite, clay and soil organic matter. The hold is weak. Held cations keep a shell of water and form no direct chemical bond with the surface, so other cations displace them easily. Some cations win more often than others: at equal amounts Al3+ replaces H+, which replaces Ca2+, then Mg2+, then K+ and NH4+, then Na+. Sheer numbers can also win. A cation added in large amounts, as in potash or lime, crowds out the rest, an effect called the law of mass action. As soil water turns more acidic, hydrogen ions take over exchange sites and push weakly held cations into solution. Plants can then use them, but they can also be leached away. Roots exploit this, making organic acids that release H+ and free cations next to the root. Exchange also buffers soil pH, alters soil structure and cleans percolating water by holding both useful and harmful cations. Because held cations resist washing downward, they preserve fertility where rainfall is moderate and temperatures are low.

soil-chem-046.title: Cation-exchange capacity, the measure of a soil's nutrient store
soil-chem-046.text: A soil's store of calcium, potassium and ammonium has a ceiling, and electric charge sets it. Cation-exchange capacity, or CEC, measures how many positively charged ions a soil can hold on the surfaces of its particles. Negative charges on those surfaces bind the cations but let them swap with others in the surrounding soil water. CEC is the exchangeable positive charge per mass of soil, usually given in centimoles of charge per kilogram, cmolc/kg. Older texts use the equivalent me/100g or meq/100g. Because it counts charge, a CEC of 10 cmolc/kg could hold 10 cmol of singly charged Na+ per kilogram. It could hold only 5 cmol of doubly charged Ca2+. Most of the charge sits on clay minerals and soil organic matter. So CEC is usually highest near the surface, where soil organic matter is richest, and falls with depth. Soils differ enormously. Measured at pH 7, average CEC in US soils runs from 3.5 cmolc/kg in {{ref:soil-class-104}} through 18.7 in {{ref:soil-class-101}} and 35.6 in {{ref:soil-class-106}} to 128 in {{ref:soil-class-098}}. Parent material and the conditions of formation set a soil's CEC. The same factors set its pH, which has a major influence on CEC in turn. Hot, wet climates leach and decompose fast, leaving little clay or soil organic matter, which explains the apparent infertility of tropical soils. CEC therefore serves as a measure of fertility. It shows how well a soil keeps nutrients such as K+, NH4+ and Ca2+ within reach of plants. It also shows how much of a pollutant cation such as Pb2+ the soil can hold.

soil-chem-053.title: Anion-exchange capacity, the smaller store for nitrate and phosphate
soil-chem-053.text: In most soils, cation-exchange capacity far exceeds its mirror image. Anion-exchange capacity, or AEC, is a soil's ability to hold negatively charged ions, such as nitrate and phosphate, on positively charged surfaces and release them later by exchange. Kaolinite, allophane and iron and aluminum oxides often carry positive surface charges. Amorphous and sesquioxide clays have the highest AEC, followed by iron oxides, and colloids with low CEC tend to have some AEC. Iron and aluminum hydroxide clays can swap their own hydroxide anions for other anions. Anions are held with decreasing strength from phosphate (H2PO4−) to sulfate, nitrate and chloride, so phosphates tend to stay on exchange sites. Exchangeable anions amount to tenths to a few milliequivalents per 100 g of dry soil. In highly weathered soils such as ferralsols, or {{ref:soil-class-103}}, AEC can exceed CEC. AEC falls as pH rises, because the extra hydroxyls push anions off colloids into solution.

soil-chem-052.title: Base saturation: how much of the exchange holds nutrients
soil-chem-052.text: Take a soil with a CEC of 20 meq, 5 meq of it held by aluminum and hydronium. Its base saturation is 15 ÷ 20 × 100% = 75%. Base saturation is the percentage of the CEC occupied by the base cations Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+. They are called base cations because they are non-acidic, not because they are bases in the usual chemical sense. Hydronium, the hydrogen ion in water, together with aluminum and iron, makes up the acid-forming cations. Base saturation rises almost in direct proportion to pH. It indexes how weathered a soil is and how available its exchangeable cation nutrients are to plants. It also helps work out how much lime a soil needs. That sum must count the acid cations held on colloids, called exchangeable acidity, not only those in the soil water. Soil classes turn on it. {{ref:soil-class-090}} have at least 35% base saturation, the more leached {{ref:soil-class-104}} less than 35%, and {{ref:soil-class-101}} more than 50%.

soil-chem-055.title: The base-cation saturation ratio and its 'ideal' soil
soil-chem-055.text: From the late 1930s, William Albrecht in Missouri set out an ideal balance for the cations on a soil's exchange sites. The base-cation saturation ratio, or BCSR, interprets soil tests by adjusting cations to such 'ideal' ratios. Albrecht's ideal was H 10%, Ca 60 to 75%, Mg 10 to 20%, K 2 to 5%, Na 0.5 to 5.0% and other cations 5%. F.E. Bear's 1945 bulletin with Prince and Malcolm proposed 65% Ca, 10% Mg, 5% K and 20% H. Most university laboratories instead simply keep each nutrient between deficiency and excess. Supporters say balanced ratios improve crops, livestock and soil life, but controlled studies disagree. Trials saw no yield difference across ratios so long as calcium dominated. Albrecht did not control pH, and much of his evidence is explained by it. A 3-year SARE trial found BCSR fertilizer cost $9.27 per acre more each year with no higher yield.

soil-chem-051.title: Measuring CEC by flooding the soil with one cation
soil-chem-051.text: To count the cations a soil holds, chemists evict them all. A concentrated solution of one cation displaces every bound cation, and the lab measures either the displaced cations or the added cation retained. Barium (Ba2+) and ammonium (NH4+) are frequent choices, though many other methods exist. Because CEC depends on pH, it is often measured in a buffer at a set pH. This potential CEC misstates the real value when the buffer's pH differs from the soil's. Effective CEC, measured at the soil's own pH, is closer to the real value but makes soils harder to compare. Applications of CaCO3 and CaSO4 can lead to an overestimate.

soil-chem-050.title: The diffuse double layer, a cloud of ions around every clay
soil-chem-050.text: Clay platelets are never bare in soil water. Each is wrapped in a diffuse double layer: two parallel layers of charge, the surface charge itself and a loosely held layer of attracted ions that screens it. Exchangeable cations sit in that outer layer, held by electric attraction but kept moving by thermal motion rather than bonded to the surface. Double layers matter most where surface area is large relative to volume, as in colloids. Adding salt thins the layer and destabilizes the colloid. In {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, abundant Na+ crowds into the double layer of clay particles and displaces Ca2+, raising the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}.

soil-chem-054.title: Base-rich and base-poor ground
soil-chem-054.text: Ground over limestone is base-rich, and ground over granite is base-poor. Base-richness is the level of chemical bases, such as calcium, potassium or magnesium ions, in soil or water. Bases neutralize acids, so base-rich places are neutral or alkaline, with pH above 7. Maritime settings are base-rich, while sandstone and ground fed only by rainfall are base-poor. A higher CEC lets a soil hold more base cations. Yet base-richness shows no correlation with available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

soil-chem-057.title: Thomas Way and the discovery of cation exchange
soil-chem-057.text: The finding that soils swap cations came from Rothamsted Experimental Station in the 19th century. There, Thomas Way and John Bennet Lawes showed that soils exchange cations. Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society in England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions. He is considered the father of soil chemistry. William Albrecht is sometimes credited with the discovery. He may only have been the first to link cation exchange with colloidal clay particles.

openers.charge-and-nutrient-holding: Most soil organic matter is dark, decay-resistant material left after biomass has been broken down and transformed over long periods. That material and the edges of clay carry electrical charge that changes with the soil's pH, and at one particular pH a surface's net charge falls to zero. Charged surfaces let one substance attach to another, and some molecules grip metal atoms at two or more points, like a claw. Living things make such molecules, and fertilizer makers use them to deliver manganese, iron, zinc and copper. This chapter follows those charges from the chemistry of humic material to the nutrients a soil can hold for plants.

reviews.charge-and-nutrient-holding: A soil holds nutrients because its surfaces carry charge. Some of that charge is permanent, built into clay crystals by substitution, while variable charge on clay edges and organic matter grows as pH rises and vanishes at a surface's point of zero charge. Humic substances supply 50 to 90% of a soil's cation-exchange capacity and also grip metals by chelation, as do the chelators made by microbes and by fertilizer makers. Cation exchange lets the stored calcium, potassium and ammonium trade places with the soil water, and base saturation shows how much of that capacity holds nutrients rather than acid. Yet the humic substances at the center of the story remain contested, since they may be partly products of the alkaline extraction used to find them.
